word:hebrew:H1015.explanation: The Hebrew word refers to “Beth,” functioning as part of a proper place name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Bible corpus represented here, it is counted twice, both within Jeremiah 48:22. No short definition or gloss is available, so the clearest supported meaning is the name itself: “Beth.” Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the complete place name in which it appears.

word:hebrew:H1059.explanation: This Hebrew word means “weeping,” referring to the act or expression of crying. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ezra 10:1, so its documented use is limited to that single passage. The word identifies weeping as something expressed or present in the passage, while the surrounding verse determines its precise force there. It is best understood simply as a term for weeping, without extending it to additional meanings not established by its recorded use.

word:hebrew:H1176.explanation: Baal-Zebub is the name of a deity of Ekron.

word:hebrew:H1198.explanation: Ba'ar means brutish or foolish, describing someone as lacking human understanding.

word:hebrew:H1257.explanation: Barbur means a fowl fattened on grain.

word:hebrew:H1323.explanation: Bath means daughter, used for a daughter in a family relationship.

word:hebrew:H1385.explanation: Gbinah means curdled milk and can also refer to cheese.

word:hebrew:H1428.explanation: This Hebrew word is a rare term whose precise meaning cannot be stated from the available lexical information alone. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 12:15, and no English meaning or short definition is provided for it. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain its role there, but the word’s basic sense remains unidentified here.

word:hebrew:H1464.explanation: Guwd means to crowd upon or attack. It describes invading people and overcoming an opponent.

word:hebrew:H1600.explanation: Gaʿa means to bellow, as cattle do.

word:hebrew:H1697.explanation: Dabar means a word or saying. It can also refer to a matter, such as one presented for judgment.

word:hebrew:H1709.explanation: Dâg means fish, including fish viewed collectively.

word:hebrew:H1745.explanation: Dumah means silence. It can also figuratively refer to death.

word:hebrew:H184.explanation: Avah means to extend or mark out.

word:hebrew:H1877.explanation: Deshe means tender grass or herb.

word:hebrew:H2003.explanation: Hamas means a dry twig or brushwood. It can also mean melting.

word:hebrew:H2182.explanation: Zanoach is the name of two places in Palestine.

word:hebrew:H2212.explanation: Zaqaq means to refine or purify something, making it clear and free of impurities.

word:hebrew:H2308.explanation: Chadal means to stop, cease, or leave off. It can also describe something as unoccupied.

word:hebrew:H243.explanation: “Aznoth” is a proper place-name, identifying a location rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, it occurs twice, both within Joshua 19:34, and the name appears as part of the place-name Aznoth Tabor. Its role is geographic identification, not a general word with a broad abstract meaning. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain its particular role in that passage.

word:hebrew:H2490.explanation: Châlal means to begin. It can also mean to profane or defile something holy.

word:hebrew:H2542.explanation: Chammuwq means a wrapping or drawers in a body-related context.

word:hebrew:H2616.explanation: Chasad means to act kindly or mercifully.

word:hebrew:H2735.explanation: The word “Hor” is a Hebrew place-name, referring to a location rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs four times, all within two verses in Numbers: 33:32 and 33:33. The name identifies a particular location in those passages. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, its precise significance in each occurrence must be understood from the larger passage.

word:hebrew:H2779.explanation: Choreph means the cold season, especially winter. It can also refer figuratively to a stage of life, including youth.

word:hebrew:H2836.explanation: Chashaq means to cling or join. It can also express love, delight, or desire.

word:hebrew:H2894.explanation: This Hebrew verb means “sweep.” It describes the action of clearing or removing something by sweeping. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Isaiah 14:23. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is an active removal by sweeping rather than a person, object, or place. This is a rare word in the Hebrew Scriptures, so its normal meaning is established by its single recorded use and consistent rendering.

word:hebrew:H2973.explanation: Ya'al means to be foolish. It can describe acting foolishly or becoming foolish.

word:hebrew:H2999.explanation: This word is the name “Jabbok,” a geographical name used in the Hebrew Old Testament. It identifies the same named location wherever it appears, rather than expressing an action, quality, or teaching. The word occurs seven times, from Genesis through Judges, and is associated with passages that command concerning it, give it to others, or mention it in speech. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:hebrew:H3040.explanation: Jedidah is a personal name. It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object, so it functions as a name within the sentence. This Hebrew word appears once in the Old Testament corpus, in 2 Kings 22:1, and is rendered “Jedidah” in the available English versions. The precise relationship of the person named to the surrounding people depends on the verse text and context, but the word itself serves as an identifying name.

word:hebrew:H3105.explanation: Yuwbal means a stream or river.

word:hebrew:H3149.explanation: This Hebrew word is a personal name rather than a common word with a clear everyday definition. Its exact sense or name meaning cannot be stated securely here because no gloss, short definition, or approved fallback meaning is available. In the Hebrew Bible corpus, it occurs twice, both within the single reference 1 Chronicles 12:2. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the person’s role there, but it would not establish an additional lexical meaning for the name.

word:hebrew:H3224.explanation: This Hebrew word is the name “Jemimah.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs only once, in Job 42:14. The available English rendering preserves the word as “Jemimah,” rather than translating it into an ordinary English concept. Thus, its primary meaning is its use as a personal name. Its particular significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself serves to identify the named individual.

word:hebrew:H3251.explanation: This Hebrew word means “poured,” expressing the action of causing something to flow out. It describes an action, not a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Exodus 30:32, and its English rendering there is “poured.” Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is the act of pouring something out. This is the word’s only recorded occurrence in the Hebrew Old Testament.

word:hebrew:H3268.explanation: Jaaziel is the name of an Israelite.

word:hebrew:H3286.explanation: Yaaph means to tire or become weary. It can also describe fainting.

word:hebrew:H3332.explanation: Yatsaq means to pour out; it can also describe casting metal or setting something firmly in place. It is used for pouring oil and for casting bronze sockets.

word:hebrew:H34.explanation: Ebyon means destitute, describing someone who is poor or needy.

word:hebrew:H3453.explanation: Yashish means an old or very aged man.

word:hebrew:H3501.explanation: Ithra is a personal name, functioning as a person’s designation rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Samuel 17:25, and the English rendering is consistently “Ithra.” Because it is a name, its meaning here is primarily identification: it points to a particular individual. The surrounding verse is needed to explain that person’s role in the passage; the name itself does not describe that role.

word:hebrew:H3538.explanation: This Hebrew word means “lying.” It expresses the idea of falsehood rather than truth. In the Hebrew Bible, it appears only once, at Daniel 2:9, so that single occurrence does not establish a broad range of uses. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical sense is the act or condition of lying.

word:hebrew:H3691.explanation: Kisleu means the ninth Hebrew month.

word:hebrew:H3747.explanation: Kerith is the name of a brook, rendered Cherith in English.

word:hebrew:H377.explanation: Iysh means to act in a manly way, or to show oneself a man.

word:hebrew:H3804.explanation: Kether means a crown or diadem, a royal circlet.

word:hebrew:H3871.explanation: This Hebrew word means “tablets” or “tables,” referring to flat objects used for writing or engraving. In the Old Testament, it most often describes the stone tablets associated with God’s commandments, including the tablets given to Moses and placed in the ark. Thus, the word identifies a physical writing surface, while its recurring setting connects it especially with God’s written covenant instructions. It occurs 43 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with many appearances in Exodus and Deuteronomy.

word:hebrew:H3952.explanation: Laqaq means to lick. It can also describe lapping water with the tongue.

word:hebrew:H4001.explanation: Mebusah means a trampling, or treading down.

word:hebrew:H4074.explanation: Madai is the name of a country in central Asia. English Scripture also renders this name as “Madai,” “Medes,” or “Media.”

word:hebrew:H4153.explanation: Moadiah is a personal name, identifying an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. Its ordinary English rendering is “Moadiah.” This Hebrew name appears once in the Old Testament corpus, in Nehemiah 12:17. Because no brief definition or explanatory meaning is provided, the name should be understood primarily as an identifying designation. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being named there.

word:hebrew:H4247.explanation: Mechillah means a cavern or cave.

word:hebrew:H427.explanation: This Hebrew noun means “oak,” referring to a particular kind of large tree. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Joshua 24:26. The word functions as a name for the physical tree itself rather than as an action, quality, or abstract idea. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary lexical meaning is simply an oak. The word’s repeated rendering as “oak” supports this clear, concrete sense.

word:hebrew:H4391.explanation: Melâ means to fill. It can also describe something being full.

word:hebrew:H4405.explanation: Millâh means a word. It can also refer to discourse or talk.

word:hebrew:H4632.explanation: Mearah is a Hebrew place-name, preserved as “Mearah” rather than translated into an ordinary descriptive word. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Joshua 13:4, so its normal lexical use is limited to that single recorded occurrence. The available wording identifies the term as a name, but without the verse text it does not establish a broader abstract meaning or additional senses. Its precise significance in Joshua depends on the surrounding passage.

word:hebrew:H4724.explanation: Miqvah means a collection of water, such as a reservoir; it can also refer to a ditch.

word:hebrew:H4751.explanation: Mar means bitter, literally or figuratively, and can also refer to bitterness.

word:hebrew:H4768.explanation: Marbîyth means increase. It can also refer to a multitude or to the offspring of a household. In a financial setting, it specifically means interest on capital.

word:hebrew:H4786.explanation: This Hebrew word means “grief,” functioning as a noun that names an experience or condition rather than an action. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Genesis 26:35. The word’s basic sense is therefore clear, while its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and verse text. Its single occurrence indicates a specific, uncommon word rather than a broad term repeatedly used throughout the Hebrew Scriptures.

word:hebrew:H4892.explanation: The Hebrew word means “destroying.” It functions as a descriptive word, identifying someone or something engaged in destroying. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ezekiel 9:1. Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, its exact force in that sentence must be understood from the passage itself; the lexical idea remains the activity of destroying. In that occurrence, it is connected with a spoken command, helping identify what is being addressed or appointed in the command.

word:hebrew:H5019.explanation: Nebuchadnezzar is the name of the king of Babylon.

word:hebrew:H5055.explanation: Nagach means to butt or push with the horns. Figuratively, it can describe warring against enemies.

word:hebrew:H5172.explanation: Nachash means to divine or use enchantments. It can also describe diligent observation.

word:hebrew:H5217.explanation: Naka means to smite, that is, drive away.

word:hebrew:H522.explanation: This word is the proper name “Ammah,” identifying a specific named referent rather than describing a general person, object, or action. It appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 2 Samuel 2:24. In that verse, it functions as the object connected with other Hebrew words in the sentence. Because no broader definition or additional occurrences are available, its normal meaning is best understood simply as the name “Ammah.”

word:hebrew:H5280.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to the group called “Naamites.” It is a group designation rather than a description of an action or quality. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Numbers 26:40, and identifies people known by this name. Its basic meaning is therefore a designation for the Naamites; the surrounding verse is needed to explain its specific role in that passage.

word:hebrew:H5363.explanation: This Hebrew word means “shaking,” describing movement marked by trembling or repeated motion. It functions as a word for the act or condition of shaking rather than naming a person, place, or object. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Isaiah. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central meaning remains the idea of shaking.

word:hebrew:H5433.explanation: Saba means to drink to satiety, filling oneself with strong drink. It can also describe becoming tipsy.

word:hebrew:H5495.explanation: “Sur” is the meaning represented by this Hebrew word in its one Old Testament occurrence. It functions as a named designation rather than as a broad everyday action or idea. The word appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 2 Kings 11:6, so its precise reference belongs to that passage’s surrounding context. The available rendering presents it as “Sur,” without an additional lexical definition.

word:hebrew:H5518.explanation: Sîr means a pot. The word can refer to a vessel used for cooking.

word:hebrew:H5521.explanation: Sukkah means a hut or booth.

word:hebrew:H5554.explanation: Sela is the name of a rock-city.

word:hebrew:H5770.explanation: This Hebrew word means “eyed,” describing the act of directing one’s eyes toward someone or something. It functions as a verb, expressing what a person does with focused visual attention. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at 1 Samuel 18:9. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the act of looking attentively or watching through one’s eyes.

word:hebrew:H5802.explanation: Azbuk is a Hebrew personal name, not a common word with an ordinary English meaning. It is rendered “Azbuk” and occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Nehemiah 3:16. Because it is a name, its meaning is primarily its identification of a person rather than a description of an action, quality, or object. The surrounding verse context would be needed to explain the individual’s role there.

word:hebrew:H5950.explanation: This Hebrew word is a rare term whose precise meaning cannot be stated securely from the available lexical information. It occurs only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Jeremiah 32:19, and no approved gloss or meaning term is available. The word functions as an object in a sentence involving giving, but that relationship alone does not establish its lexical sense. Its exact meaning therefore must be determined from the full verse and surrounding passage rather than from the word record by itself.

word:hebrew:H6043.explanation: This word is a Hebrew personal name rendered “Anaiah.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Nehemiah: Nehemiah 8:4 and 10:22. Since it functions as a name, its ordinary significance here is to identify Anaiah; the surrounding verse is needed to explain that person’s specific role.

word:hebrew:H614.explanation: The Hebrew word refers to an “ingathering,” the gathering in of what has grown or been produced. It names a seasonal gathering rather than the act of sowing or planting. In the Old Testament evidence available here, it occurs twice, both in Exodus: once in Exodus 23:16 and once in Exodus 34:22. In both places, the word is connected with the yearly cycle of cultivation and gathering. Its precise force in either verse is clarified by the surrounding passage.

word:hebrew:H6177.explanation: Aroër is the name of three places in or near Palestine.

word:hebrew:H6326.explanation: Puah is a personal name, rendered “Puah” in English. It identifies a woman mentioned once in the Hebrew Bible, in Exodus 1:15. As a name rather than a descriptive word, it identifies the individual being addressed or discussed in that passage. The available wording does not provide an additional lexical definition, so its plain role is to name Puah. Understanding what she does or how she relates to others requires the surrounding verse and passage.

word:hebrew:H6384.explanation: “Palluites” is a designation for people identified by that name. It is not presented here as an action, quality, or general object, but as a people-name used in the Hebrew Old Testament. This word occurs once, in Numbers 26:5, and the English rendering is “Palluites.” Without the surrounding verse text, its precise role in that passage cannot be explained further; its ordinary lexical function is to identify the Palluites.

word:hebrew:H6414.explanation: Palil means a magistrate or judge.

word:hebrew:H6458.explanation: This Hebrew verb means “Hew,” an action-word describing material being worked by striking or cutting it. It is used for deliberate shaping work, including the preparation of stone tablets and building-related labor. The word appears six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its basic sense is consistent but its precise force depends on what material and task the surrounding sentence describes.

word:hebrew:H6461.explanation: Pasas means to disappear or cease.

word:hebrew:H6520.explanation: Perazon means leadership or rule and can refer concretely to rulers.

word:hebrew:H658.explanation: Ephes-Dammim is the name of a place.

word:hebrew:H6627.explanation: This Hebrew word is a verb meaning “cometh,” describing an action in which something comes or proceeds. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, once in Deuteronomy 23:13 and once in Ezekiel 4:12. Its basic role is to express movement or arrival rather than name a person, object, or quality. The precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

word:hebrew:H6722.explanation: Tsîydônîy means a Sidonian, an inhabitant of Sidon.

word:hebrew:H6876.explanation: Tsorî means a person of Tyre, or an inhabitant of Tyre.

word:hebrew:H6898.explanation: This Hebrew noun refers to a “pavilion,” an enclosed shelter or structure. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Numbers 25:8. Because the word appears only there and the verse text is not included here, its precise role in that sentence depends on the surrounding passage. Its basic meaning is therefore a named place or structure: a pavilion, rather than an action, quality, or person. The word’s recorded use is singular within the Hebrew corpus.

word:hebrew:H6915.explanation: Qadad means to bow or bend the head or body in deference.

word:hebrew:H6959.explanation: This Hebrew word means “helmet,” a piece of protective equipment worn on the head. It functions as the name of a physical object, not an action or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice: in 1 Samuel 17:38 and Ezekiel 23:24. Both occurrences place the helmet among objects involved in giving or being handled, fitting its ordinary sense as head protection. Its precise role in either verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:hebrew:H7066.explanation: Qena means to purchase or buy.

word:hebrew:H7088.explanation: Qaphad means to contract or roll together, and it can also mean to cut off.

word:hebrew:H7192.explanation: Qesitah means an ingot estimated and stamped for use as a coin, or a piece of silver money. It refers to money paid for land and to a piece of money given to Job.

word:hebrew:H720.explanation: Arod is a Hebrew name rendered in English as “Arod.” It functions as a proper name rather than an ordinary descriptive word. This word appears once in the Hebrew Bible corpus, at Numbers 26:17. Because no short definition or wider usage is provided, its meaning is limited to identifying the person or group bearing this name; the surrounding verse would be needed to explain that reference further.

word:hebrew:H7237.explanation: Rabbah is a place name. In Scripture, it identifies a city of the children of Ammon.

word:hebrew:H7325.explanation: This Hebrew verb means “run.” It describes an action or movement, functioning as a predicate rather than as the name of a person, object, or condition. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at Leviticus 15:3. Because the available wording is brief and the verse text is not included here, the surrounding passage determines exactly what is running in that occurrence; the basic verbal idea remains “run.”

word:hebrew:H7383.explanation: Riphah means pounded grits, referring to ground grain such as corn or wheat.

word:hebrew:H7404.explanation: Rekullah means trade as peddled, or merchandise.

word:hebrew:H7448.explanation: Resen means a halter or bridle used for restraint.

word:hebrew:H7552.explanation: Rekem is a Hebrew proper name, rendered “Rekem.” It identifies a named individual or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The word occurs six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages that record genealogical relationships and births. Because no short definition is given, its meaning is chiefly its identity as the name Rekem within those passages.

word:hebrew:H7710.explanation: This Hebrew word means “blasted.” It describes something affected by a destructive condition, especially in the language of Genesis 41. The word appears three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Genesis 41:6, 41:23, and 41:27. In each occurrence, it functions as a describing word connected with other features of the dream’s imagery. Its precise force in each verse is understood from the surrounding passage, but its central idea is being blasted or rendered unproductive.

word:hebrew:H7787.explanation: This word expresses a limited idea whose exact sense depends on its context. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 20:3. No direct English meaning or short definition is available here, so its precise ordinary sense cannot be stated responsibly from the word alone. The surrounding verse and its relationship to nearby words are necessary for a fuller understanding. Its role is identified as expressing an action or assertion within that passage, but the verse text itself must supply the specific meaning.

word:hebrew:H78.explanation: This Hebrew word is the personal name Ibzan, referring to a man rather than describing a general quality or action. It occurs twice in the Old Testament, both times in Judges 12:8 and 12:10. The surrounding scriptural record associates Ibzan with judging Israel and later records his death and burial. Since it functions as a proper name, its meaning for readers is primarily identification: it tells us which person is being discussed, rather than supplying a translatable concept such as an object, action, or virtue.

word:hebrew:H7853.explanation: Satan means to attack. It can also describe resisting someone as an adversary.

word:hebrew:H7901.explanation: Shakab means to lie down. It can also describe sexual relations, as in the words, “Lie with me.”

word:hebrew:H7974.explanation: Shelah is a personal name, rendered “Shelah” in the Hebrew Old Testament. It identifies a man listed within genealogies, especially the family lines traced in Genesis and 1 Chronicles. The name appears nine times across seven verses, and its surrounding SEE connections consistently place it in birth and begetting records. Thus, this word functions as a person’s name rather than as a general description or action. Its exact significance in any particular genealogy comes from the names and relationships stated in that passage.

word:hebrew:H8016.explanation: Shillemites is a Hebrew group name identifying people known by that designation. It functions as a plural name for a people or family group, rather than as a description of an action or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at Numbers 26:49. The available English rendering preserves the designation as “Shillemites,” so its basic meaning is the name of this identified group; the surrounding verse would be needed to explain its specific role there.

word:hebrew:H8179.explanation: Sha'ar means an opening, such as a gate.

word:hebrew:H8193.explanation: Saphah means lip. It can also refer to speech. It can also refer to a brim.

word:hebrew:H8207.explanation: Shephiphon means a kind of serpent, rendered as an adder.

word:hebrew:H823.explanation: Ashnah is a Hebrew name rendered as “Ashnah.” It functions as a proper name rather than an ordinary word describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament data, with both occurrences recorded in Joshua 15. Its exact significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the available lexical information supports treating Ashnah as a named entity, not expanding it into an additional meaning.

word:hebrew:H8290.explanation: Sharonite means an inhabitant of Sharon.

word:hebrew:H8342.explanation: Sâsôwn means cheerfulness, expressed as gladness and joy.

word:hebrew:H8412.explanation: Tadmor is the name of a place mentioned in the Hebrew Old Testament. It is rendered “Tadmor” in both of its recorded occurrences, so it functions as a proper place-name rather than a general description or action. The name appears once in 1 Kings and once in 2 Chronicles, referring to the same named location in the biblical record. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:hebrew:H8508.explanation: Toknîyth refers to a measured pattern. It can also mean a sum.

word:hebrew:H8544.explanation: Temunah means an image, likeness, or form.

word:hebrew:H8603.explanation: Tophel is a proper name, rendered “Tophel,” rather than an ordinary word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Bible, it occurs once, at Deuteronomy 1:1, so its role is that of a specific name within that passage rather than a broadly recurring Hebrew term. The available material does not establish an additional lexical meaning or explain the name’s etymology.

word:hebrew:H885.explanation: This word means “children,” functioning as a plural noun for people identified together as a family or group. It occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Deuteronomy 10:6. In this passage, the word is connected with the people called Beeroth Bene-jaakan, so it helps identify a collective group of persons rather than describing an action or quality. Its precise role in the verse depends on the surrounding context, but its basic sense is people designated together as children.

word:hebrew:H957.explanation: Baz means plunder, booty, spoil, or prey—what is taken from others, whether goods seized in war or people made prey.
